nameStory: This fungus earned its common name "Coral Spot" from the tiny, bright orange-red bumps it produces that look remarkably like miniature coral formations sprouting from dead wood. The scientific name "cinnabarina" comes from the Latin word for cinnabar, a bright red mineral, perfectly describing those eye-catching coral-colored spots that make this fungus so recognizable.
description: Coral Spot is a small fungus that creates distinctive bright orange-red bumps on dead and dying branches of broadleaf trees. These tiny, round fruiting bodies are usually only 1-2 millimeters across but often appear in clusters that can cover several inches of a branch. While it primarily feeds on dead wood as a decomposer, it can also attack living trees that are already stressed or wounded, causing cankers that girdle and kill branches.

idTips.label: Coral-colored bumps
idTips.description: Look for tiny, bright orange-red to coral-pink bumps that feel slightly rough and raised when you run your finger over them - they're firm and don't squish like berries

idTips.label: Clustered arrangement
idTips.description: The spots typically appear in loose clusters or scattered groups along dead branches, sometimes forming lines where bark meets wood

idTips.label: Host preference
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on broadleaf trees like maple, oak, and ash - you won't see this on pine or other conifers

idTips.label: Branch condition
idTips.description: Appears on recently dead branches that still have bark attached, often where the bark is starting to loosen but hasn't completely fallen off

idTips.label: Size and texture
idTips.description: Individual spots are pin-head to match-head sized with a slightly bumpy, granular surface that feels dry to the touch

habitat: Coral Spot thrives throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, from lowland woodlands to mid-elevation slopes. You'll find it on dead branches of common broadleaf trees like maples, oaks, birches, and ashes in both mature forests and suburban areas with established trees. It's particularly common along woodland edges and in parks where stressed trees provide ideal infection opportunities.

seasonality.spring: Fresh coral spots begin appearing as temperatures warm, often most vibrant and numerous on branches killed during winter storms.
seasonality.summer: Peak visibility period when the bright orange-red fruiting bodies are most abundant and colorful on recently dead wood.
seasonality.fall: Still easily spotted but older spots may fade to duller orange or brown as spores are released and the structures age.
seasonality.winter: Spots persist but become less conspicuous, often appearing darker and more weathered against snow and bare branches.

funFact: Coral Spot acts like a tree undertaker with a split personality - it patiently waits as a harmless decomposer on dead wood, but the moment a healthy tree gets wounded or stressed, it can switch to attack mode and become a aggressive parasite that kills living branches!
confusionNotes: Small orange fungi or slime molds might look similar at first glance, but Coral Spot's bumps are always firmly attached to wood and feel dry and granular - unlike squishy slime molds or other fungi that might be softer or differently textured. Remember: if it's bright coral-colored, hard, and on a dead broadleaf branch, it's likely Coral Spot.
contextualKnowledge: What appears to be a single species called "Coral Spot" is actually a complex of at least four closely related species that look nearly identical to the naked eye - scientists only discovered this in 2011 using genetic analysis, so don't worry about telling them apart in the field!
compareHints: While Nectria pseudotrichia is a close relative in the same genus, it typically produces different colored fruiting structures and has distinct microscopic features. Most other Nectria species in our region lack the distinctive bright coral-red coloration that makes Coral Spot so recognizable, often appearing as darker red, brown, or having different shaped fruiting bodies entirely.
